title: November 2, 2026 - FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality
body: FDA News Release FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality FDA issues final guidance for cell and gene therapy manufacturers, recommends building potency assurance into every stage of a therapy’s lifecycle — from early development through patient delivery For Immediate Release: November 02, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today issued final guidance for manufacturers of cellular and gene therapy (CGT) products to implement a comprehensive, science- and risk-based plan for making sure their products meet potency standards. The guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for a Potency Assurance Strategy, which guides manufacturers to test and verify — before a product reaches a patient — that every batch meets a defined standard of potency to do what the product is supposed to do therapeutically. The Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products final guidance replaces FDA's 2011 potency testing guidance for CGT products and applies to treatments for serious and often life-threatening conditions. By law, manufacturers are expected to verify that their products work as intended, from the time of approval through post-approval monitoring. This final guidance provides FDA’s current thinking and recommendations on how manufacturers can meet that requirement. "Patients who receive cellular and gene therapies are often battling serious or life-threatening conditions, such as cancers and rare diseases, and they deserve the assurance that the product administered to them will perform as intended," said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research . "This guidance reflects the FDA's commitment to ensuring America remains the best place in the world to innovate — and that innovation is matched by the highest standards of product quality and patient safety." The guidance provides flexible, risk-based recommendations for manufacturers on how to integrate potency considerations at every stage of development and commercialization — from early-phase investigational new drug (IND) submissions through biologics license application (BLA) approval and continued post-market verification. Key topics include controls for variability in raw materials, testing during manufacturing, and lab tests that confirm each batch is biologically active in a way that matches its intended therapeutic effect. The guidance also addresses specialized considerations for products with short shelf lives, viral vector gene therapies, and patient-specific therapies. By giving manufacturers a clear, predictable roadmap, this guidance supports faster access to safe and effective therapies for patients who often have no other treatment options — many of whom receive products made individually for a single person. In doing so, it advances the FDA's public health pillars: protecting patients through rigorous quality standards, promoting innovation by providing regulatory clarity, and reinforcing the integrity of the supply chain for some of the most complex medical products in existence. The FDA will host a webinar on December 10, 2026, to help stakeholders understand and implement the guidance. Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ###

title: Google Messages, Phone by Google, and Google Contacts get new, updated icons.
body: Google Messages, Phone by Google, and Google Contacts get new, updated icons. Nov 02, 2026 Starting today, we’re rolling out refreshed icons for three apps that help you stay connected: Google Messages, Phone by Google, and Google Contacts. These are the same apps you trust and use every day, now with enhanced icons designed with your feedback in mind. The new icons are sharper and clearer on your home screen. For example, we’ve added a subtle but crisp gradient with easily readable edges. They also feature updated curvature and coloring to align with the rest of the Google apps you know and love, such as our core Google logo . Don’t worry, the functionality of these apps isn’t changing as a result of the new icons. You’ll simply spot a sleeker, more cohesive look on your home screen in the coming weeks. Check out the conversation on our community forum for more.

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)
body: AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026) The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions , which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it. The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock , and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex. AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate , which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate , which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher. AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs. Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2 , and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR , point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks : lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x. Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager . Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service , producing the evidence its regulator needed. How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog. Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!
retained_feed_body: The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions , which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it. The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock , and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex. AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate , which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate , which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher. AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs. Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2 , and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR , point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks : lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x. Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager . Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service , producing the evidence its regulator needed. How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog. Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

title: U.S. Attorney Gerace announces FY2026 prosecution statistics
body: Press Release U.S. Attorney Gerace announces FY2026 prosecution statistics Monday, November 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Ohio Results include substantial increases in violent crime, gun & white-collar prosecutions CINCINNATI – U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II announced today results of the Southern District of Ohio’s continuing work to reduce violent crime, firearms offenses and fraud in fiscal year 2026. Fiscal year 2026 includes Oct. 1, 2025, through Sept. 30, 2026. Violent and Gun Crime “I am extremely proud of what my Office has accomplished since I became U.S. Attorney just over a year ago,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “My tenure began amid a significant uptick in violent and gun crimes, particularly in downtown Cincinnati, and I promised the public that we would aggressively pursue federal charges against those offenders. The statistics show that we have done just that. I asked my prosecutors to target repeat violent offenders and to focus on the safety of the streets in our communities and they continue to answer the bell.” As indicated below, in Cincinnati alone, the Office increased prosecutions of firearms offenders by 250% when compared to FY2025. More generally, violent crime prosecutions increased by 148.5% in Cincinnati and by 92.7% districtwide. The total number of defendants charged with firearms offenses and violent crimes across the District sets a Southern District of Ohio record based on available statistics going back to FY2004. The total number of defendants charged with firearms offenses represents an increase of 93.5% from FY2025. Defendants Charged with Violent Crimes Location Total Defendants Percentage Increase from FY2025 Districtwide 237 +92.7% Cincinnati 82 +148.5% Columbus 99 +67.8% Dayton 56 +80.6% Defendants Charged with Firearms Offenses (18 U.S.C. 922(g) and 924(c)) Location Total Defendants Percentage Increase from FY2025 Districtwide 236 +93.4% Cincinnati 63 +250.0% Columbus 96 +62.7% Dayton 77 +71.1% “None of these cases are possible without strong partnerships with our local, state and federal law enforcement agencies who investigate these crimes. I thank them for joining us in the fight against violence,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “I am also grateful to Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson for his continued support and for providing us with a Special Assistant United States Attorney dedicated to federal gun cases.” Fraud and White-Collar Crime “The fight against fraud, especially fraud against taxpayer-funded government benefits programs, is a top priority for this Office,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “This fiscal year, we brought charges against several individuals who allegedly stole tens of millions of dollars from government programs designed to provide healthcare and food benefits to Americans in need—including a Medicaid fraud scheme involving $30 million and a SNAP fraud scheme involving $29.7 million. We will continue to hold fraudsters accountable for stealing taxpayer dollars and for depriving vulnerable citizens of these services.” As indicated below, the District increased prosecution of white-collar defendants by 46.3% when compared to FY2025, with the largest increases coming from the Dayton and Columbus areas. Defendants Charged with White-Collar Crimes Location Total Defendants Percentage Increase from FY2025 Districtwide 60 +46.3% Cincinnati 19 +5.6% Columbus 32 +68.4% Dayton 9 +125.0% “These statistics represent just a few of the areas that our dedicated public servants focus on every day to keep the people of the Southern District of Ohio safe,” added U.S. Attorney Gerace. “In addition to violent, gun and white-collar crime, my Office remains steadfast in combatting child exploitation, protecting our homeland security, ridding our streets of deadly drugs, enforcing immigration laws, and dismantling transnational criminal organizations. We are proud to do our jobs in service to our communities and this great country.” # # # Updated November 2, 2026 Topics Benefit Fraud Financial Fraud Firearms Offenses Violent Crime Component USAO - Ohio, Southern
retained_feed_body: CINCINNATI – U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II announced today results of the Southern District of Ohio’s continuing work to reduce violent crime, firearms offenses and fraud in fiscal year 2026.

title: Chesapeake esthetician pleads guilty in laser treatment case
body: Press Release Chesapeake esthetician pleads guilty in laser treatment case Monday, November 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Virginia NORFOLK, Va. – A Chesapeake woman pled guilty to wire fraud in relation to falsely representing her credentials to provide hair and tattoo removal by laser. According to court documents, Hayley Nicole Atwood, 33, was licensed by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation as a basic esthetician. Beginning in at least 2017, Atwood consistently falsely purported to be a master esthetician to colleagues and potential customers. Under Virginia law, master estheticians may perform more advanced procedures such as laser hair removal or laser tattoo removal, but only if properly trained and supervised by a licensed physician or physician assistant. Atwood owned and operated esthetics spas in Chesapeake, Virginia, and Elizabeth City, North Carolina. In March and April of 2021, Atwood purchased two Spectrum Laser devices for her spas. Atwood employed a medical director from December 2019 through July 2021 and a second medical director from July 2021 through November 2022. Neither medical director ever supervised or authorized Atwood or anyone at her business to perform laser tattoo removal. The second director supervised laser hair removal but never evaluated Atwood or her staff or saw her patients. Atwood consistently advertised, offered, and performed laser tattoo and hair removal. Several of Atwood’s clients suffered injury as a result of her laser treatments, including burning and scarring. Atwood is scheduled to be sentenced on March 5, 2027, and faces up to 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia; Marie Maguire, Special Agent in Charge, FDA Office of Criminal Investigations, Metro Washington Field Office; and Col. Jeffrey S. Katz, Superintendent of Virginia State Police, made the announcement after U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas E. Miller accepted the plea. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kristen S. Taylor and Rebecca Gantt are prosecuting the case. Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:26-cr-83. Contact USAVAE.Press@usdoj.gov Updated November 2, 2026 Topic Fraud Component USAO - Virginia, Eastern

title: Rosebud Woman Sentenced to Federal Prison for Involuntary Manslaughter
body: Press Release Rosebud Woman Sentenced to Federal Prison for Involuntary Manslaughter Monday, November 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a Rosebud, South Dakota, woman convicted of Involuntary Manslaughter. The sentencing took place on October 26, 2026. Crystal McCloskey, age 34, was sentenced to two years and four months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. McCloskey was indicted by a federal grand jury in January 2026. She pleaded guilty on July 29, 2026. On June 14, 2025, McCloskey was under the influence of alcohol and controlled substances and drove her vehicle at a high rate of speed.  McCloskey missed a curve near Rosebud and drove off the road.  The vehicle rolled, throwing McCloskey and her passenger out of the vehicle.  The passenger died as a result of her injuries in the crash.  The offense occurred in the Rosebud Sioux Indian Reservation. This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in Federal court as opposed to State court. This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kimberly Zachrison prosecuted the case. McCloskey was ordered to self-surrender to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service on November 10, 2026. Contact usasd.press@usdoj.gov Updated November 2, 2026 Topic Indian Country Law and Justice Component USAO - South Dakota

title: Large-Scale Bastrop Methamphetamine Distributor Sentenced to 28 Years in Federal Prison
body: Press Release Large-Scale Bastrop Methamphetamine Distributor Sentenced to 28 Years in Federal Prison Monday, November 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Louisiana MONROE – On October 21, 2026, United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty sentenced Justavious K. “Tae Tae” Williams , 25, of Bastrop, to 336 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Possess a Controlled Substance with Intent to Distribute and for Possessing a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Crime, followed by five years of supervised release. Williams previously pled guilty to the charges on July 10, 2026. According to court documents, between May 16, 2025, and October 9, 2025, Williams participated in a methamphetamine trafficking organization. Investigators executed a wiretap on one of Williams’ co-conspirator’s phones and intercepted calls and messages in which Williams discussed acquiring and distributing large quantities of methamphetamine. On October 1, 2025, communications revealed that Williams’ co-conspirators were arranging the pickup of a large shipment of methamphetamine from Texas. Williams then traveled to Garland, Texas, where agents observed him and a co-conspirator load a bright orange suitcase into a vehicle. After the vehicle returned to Louisiana, Louisiana State Police (LSP) later attempted a traffic stop. Williams fled the stop, leading troopers on a brief pursuit before Williams and the co-conspirator were caught and arrested. A search of the vehicle revealed approximately 25 kilograms of methamphetamine in the suitcase. Roughly a week later, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agents executed a search warrant at a local address where Williams was found with the same co-conspirator as in the car stop. Inside the residence, agents recovered seven firearms along with various quantities of ecstasy pills, methamphetamine, marijuana, and other controlled substances. A cook lab trailer located behind the residence contained 20,000 methamphetamine pills and more than three kilograms of additional powder methamphetamine. U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement. The case was investigated by DEA, LSP, and Monroe Metro Narcotics. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Aaron Crawford with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan. You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla. Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 3:25 cr 299. ### CONTACT: Public Affairs: Cara.Alexander@usdoj.gov United States Attorney’s Office: www.justice.gov/usao-wdla (337) 262-6704 Updated November 2, 2026 Topic Drug Trafficking Components Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) USAO - Louisiana, Western

title: Boris Vujčić: Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world
body:
Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Boris Vujčić Vice-President of the European Central Bank SPEECH Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world Speech by Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB, at the Central Bank of Ireland’s Financial System Conference Dublin, 2 November 2026 Thank you to the Central Bank of Ireland for organising this conference and inviting me to speak. It is a great pleasure to be here in Dublin. Ireland illustrates why the topics of today’s event – from geopolitics to financial resilience – are timely. Ireland has one of the most open economies in the world and it is deeply integrated into European and global markets. It is a Single Market success story, and a reminder that openness remains one of Europe’s greatest strengths. But openness works both ways. A shift in US trade policy or a turn in global capital flows can spill over to the Irish economy particularly quickly. What is true for Ireland is also true on a larger scale for the EU, the world’s largest trading bloc. [ 1 ] So, the question I would like to discuss today is simple to ask but harder to answer: how do we retain the benefits of an open economy in a more uncertain world increasingly shaped by geopolitics? My answer in a single sentence is: not by retreating from openness, but by building the resilience that allows this openness to endure. Geopolitics is becoming economics Let me start with the environment we are facing. Geopolitical shocks are becoming more frequent. They affect growth and inflation directly, and they can threaten financial stability. We have seen this repeatedly in recent years. Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have triggered severe disruptions in energy markets. Tariffs have renewed uncertainty and redirected global trade flows, while restrictions on exports of critical technologies and raw materials have reinforced the value of strategic autonomy (Slide 2, left-hand side). Alongside these developments, we have seen sanctions regimes, cyber threats and a step change in security and defence spending. The result is a different macroeconomic environment. Inflation, for example, is now driven more often by supply shocks – in the past six years supply factors have played a role in three major shocks: in 2020, 2022 and 2026. And we are faced with more volatile energy prices as well as greater uncertainty about the outlook (Slide 2, right-hand side). These shocks can also be transmitted through financial channels. Bond and equity prices may come under pressure, while investment funds could face outflows that amplify market movements. [ 2 ] Banks exposed to affected countries, sectors or markets may experience losses that weigh on capital or raise funding costs, potentially leading them to tighten lending. [ 3 ] So far, the financial system has absorbed each of these shocks remarkably well. But financial effects can be highly non-linear and typically emerge abruptly: past resilience is no reason for complacency. Common in origin, uneven in impact We cannot prevent geopolitical shocks. And pulling back from the world would not shield us from such shocks: while a fragmenting world means fewer links, it also means that those links are more concentrated. The result is less diversification and higher risk. Energy is the clearest, and unfortunately a recurring, example. The EU imports 57% of its energy, and almost all of its oil and gas. Before 2022, much of that came from Russia. That is why Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused the EU’s largest energy shock since the 1970s. Europe responded. We diversified our energy supplies by increasing liquefied natural gas (LNG) import capacity and reduced our dependence on Russia. This is an important achievement. But diversification alone could not shield us when tensions erupted in the Middle East earlier this year. This showed us that exposure is only half the story.  The other half is about resilience – in other words, how well we absorb the shocks. For the financial sector, resilience means strong capital and liquidity buffers, diversified funding, and payment and settlement systems that can withstand operational and cyber threats. But there is also a broader, economy-wide dimension to resilience – one that is becoming increasingly important for Europe. In a more competitive and uncertain global environment, resilience requires stronger mechanisms for sharing risks and diversifying supply chains across countries and markets. Coming back to the example of the energy shocks, they hit every Member State differently. How hard they land depends on a country’s energy mix, its trade links and the structure of its financial system. Take 2022: electricity prices for firms rose far more, and stayed high far longer, in Italy than in Spain – and part of the difference is that Spain generates much more of its power from renewables (Slide 3). Two encouraging points follow from this. First, our energy supply is already more resilient than in 2022. As the energy mix shifts towards low-carbon sources, wholesale electricity prices have become less sensitive to gas prices, including since the start of the war in the Middle East. [ 4 ] Second, shocks that are common in origin but uneven in impact have already shown how European risk sharing can cushion country-specific effects and strengthen resilience across the EU. This shows that the lessons about how Europe can enhance its resilience are not the same as those for other large economies such as the United States and China, which automatically benefit from scale. Europe needs to find its strength in the depth of its integration – rising above the Member State perspective towards a truly European perspective. Europe’s untapped strength: a truly single market Today, fragmentation prevents us from realising our European potential. Too often, national rules, standards and procedures diverge, forcing companies to navigate multiple legal and regulatory regimes when they operate across borders. These differences act like internal tariffs: according to ECB estimates, they are equivalent to a tariff of around 67% for goods and 95% for services. [ 5 ] While this is the upper bound of estimates, the message is clear: doing business across borders within the Single Market is expensive. One consequence is a persistent home bias, with capital staying within national borders, alongside a growing allocation of European savings to markets outside the EU. Consider equity markets. Since 2014, estimated tariff-equivalent frictions affecting cross-border equity holdings within the euro area have fallen by around 12 percentage points. Between the euro area and the United States, the decline has been around 25 percentage points, roughly twice as much (Slide 4, left-hand side). [ 6 ] Strikingly, we are integrating faster with the United States than with each other. [ 7 ] As a result, European savings increasingly fund US companies. There are, of course, good reasons to diversify. But in a fragmenting world, this also means greater dependence on a single external partner and leaves our own markets underdeveloped. Venture capital tells a similar story: US funds invest around six times as much as EU-based funds (Slide 4, right-hand side). [ 8 ] Foreign venture capital funds partly fill the gap, but this makes it more likely that successful European start-ups move their headquarters or intellectual property abroad, or choose to list outside the EU. Beyond missing out on growth, a lack of integration weakens risk sharing and therefore resilience. Let me explain why. When a shock hits one country harder than others, integrated systems help share the burden. This holds true for energy and electricity markets, where physical interconnections and common trading hubs foster price convergence. [ 9 ] It is also true for financial markets, where investors operate across borders and regions. Cross-border investors spread gains and losses. Banks operating across borders can help sustain lending where domestic conditions are weak. The numbers are stark. ECB research finds that around 70% of state-level output shocks in the United States are absorbed through markets and fiscal transfers, with capital markets doing most of the work. In the euro area, the overall share is far lower, at around 30%, and capital markets absorb only 5 to 10%. [ 10 ] Two results show what that gap means in practice. European firms cut investment in response to higher oil prices. For US firms, we see no such reduction (Slide 5, left-hand side). [ 11 ] And among European firms most exposed to the COVID-19 shock, those with mostly domestic shareholders cut investment 20% more than their peers with an international shareholder base (Slide 5, right-hand side). [ 12 ] In a fragmented Europe, investment becomes the margin of adjustment whenever a shock hits. That is a resilience problem before it is a growth problem. Integration: our best response and the lever we control We cannot set the trade policy of others. But the openness across borders within our Single Market is entirely within our control. Our broader aim should be to reduce barriers to trade in goods and services and complete the Single Market. And the numbers are on our side. Reducing internal barriers to goods and services by just 2% could, in the long run, offset the projected impact of higher US tariffs on euro area GDP, estimated at around 0.7 percentage points between 2025 and 2027 (Slide 6). [ 13 ] This shows that integration can strengthen resilience and enhance competitiveness at the same time. And again, in light of the two consecutive energy shocks we have faced, energy provides a particularly relevant example. A more interconnected and genuinely integrated energy market, built primarily on renewables, would reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and limit their impact on electricity prices. From a central banking perspective, one of the most important building blocks of the Single Market is the savings and investments union, which targets the financial sector. I am particularly pleased that Commissioner Albuquerque is with us today, as this is a key priority on her agenda and one on which we are closely aligned. I look forward to hearing her reflections on how we can move it forward. Importantly, the savings and investments union encompasses both the banking union and the capital markets union. Cross-border banking groups should be able to operate across the euro area as though it were a single jurisdiction, with capital and liquidity moving freely within the group. That requires completing the missing pillar of the banking union – a European deposit insurance scheme – complemented by a sound crisis management framework. Deposit protection should be equally robust across the euro area, and bank failures should be managed consistently throughout the banking union, supported by more harmonised creditor hierarchies and insolvency rules. We also need a truly integrated European capital market that mobilises savings for productive investment and allows capital to flow freely across the EU. Harmonising withholding taxes is an important part of that effort. And finally, the Single Market cannot function without resilient payment systems. This is why Europe needs its own resilient payments infrastructure: one that keeps working under stress and is European. The digital euro is part of the answer, reducing reliance on non-European retail payment providers. Another part is a European infrastructure for wholesale digital payments. In this regard, the launch of Pontes in September marked an important milestone. Each of these initiatives lowers barriers and makes Europe more integrated and resilient. Together, they help ensure that Europe stays open to the world. Conclusion Let me conclude. The geopolitical environment is unlikely to become any easier. But how well we absorb the shocks we face depends very much on the choices we make. Openness, integration and resilience are not competing goals. They reinforce one another. Integration makes us more resilient. Resilience allows us to remain open. And openness, as Ireland’s experience shows, is one of Europe’s greatest sources of prosperity. Thank you for your attention. Trade openness, measured as the sum of gross exports and imports over output, is significantly higher in the euro area than in the United States. body: October 30, 2026 Washington – Fial data from an annual survey of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 were released today and posted on the Treasury web site at https://home.treasury.gov/data/treasury-international-capital-tic-system/tic-forms-instructions/us-claims-on-foreigners-from-holdings-of-foreign-securities .  Preliminary data were released and posted on the Treasury web site on August 31, 2025. The survey was undertaken jointly by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. A complementary survey measuring foreign portfolio holdings of U.S. securities also occurs annually.  Data from the most recent such survey, for securities held at end-June 2026, are currently being processed.  Preliminary results are expected to be reported on February 26, 2027. Overall Results This survey measured the value of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 as approximately $19.3 trillion, with $15.2 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.6 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities (original term-to-maturity in excess of one year), and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The previous such survey, conducted as of year-end 2024, measured U.S. holdings of approximately $15.8 trillion, with $12.1 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.3 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities, and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The increase in U.S. holdings of foreign securities in 2025 was mainly in equity (see Table 1). U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities by country at the end of 2025 were the largest for the Cayman Islands ($3.1 trillion), followed by the United Kingdom ($2.0 trillion), Canada ($1.9 trillion), and Japan ($1.5 trillion) (see Table 2).
